title: Two-vortex scattering: solitons, factorization, and channel decay
html:
The channel algebra developed in the two-vortex proposition governs the scattering theory of interacting vortex loops.

The R-matrix as the two-vortex S-matrix. Two geodesic vortices — soliton critical points of \mathcal{E}_q that devolve to Hasimoto solitons at q \to 1 — interact exclusively via the braid operator of the R-matrix braiding. The Yang--Baxter equation codifies the complete factorization of the multi-vortex scattering event. A three-loop interaction remains strictly independent of the internal ordering of pairwise exchanges. The loops transit each other acquiring only channel phase shifts, never generating internal-state debris. This factorization mathematically guarantees that the weak scattering event cannot shred the internal dynamics of an individual loop.

The Hopf link as the minimal scattering event. Two loops bearing linking number one complete the braid \sigma_1^2. Per the spectral square proposition, the interaction decomposes over the Hopf channel pair into \sigma_1^2 = q^2 e_+ + q^{-2} e_-. The Hopf link demands zero hyperbolic volume, perfectly mirroring the soliton constraint: the two loops perturb each other's trajectories while avoiding strictly bonded volume.

Channel decay equals the eigenvalue ratio. At each crossing, the antisymmetric channel carries weight -q^{-1} against the symmetric channel's weight q. This extracts a relative ratio of -q^{-2} (eigenvalue-ratio identity). At the physical substrate anchor q_0 > 1, this ratio represents a strict contraction, q_0^{-2} \approx 0.81. Every crossing diminishes the antisymmetric perturbation by nearly twenty percent. Bound alongside the gapped second variation of \mathcal{E}_q (geodesic vortices), this defines the dual mechanism guaranteeing soliton stability: the substrate exponentially dampens inter-loop disturbances at every crossing, while the spectral gap isolates disturbances within the loops themselves.
